entries.5462eb43d798643119536d6b015f0c8bb04cf446: <div sID="gen18879" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="24" osisID="Ezek.24" sID="Ezek.24"/> <div eID="gen18879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18880" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18881" type="x-p"/> Here are two sermons in this chapter, preached on a particular occasion, and they are both from Mount Sinai, the mount of terror, both from Mount Ebal, the mount of curses; both speak the approaching fate of Jerusalem. The occasion of them was the king of Babylon's laying siege to Jerusalem, and the design of them is to show that in the issue of that siege he should be not only master of the place, but destroyer of it. I. By the sign of flesh boiling in a pot over the fire are shown the miseries that Jerusalem should suffer during the siege, and justly, for her filthiness, <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.1-Ezek.24.14">ver. 1-14</reference>. II. By the sign of Ezekiel's not mourning for the death of his wife is shown that the calamities coming upon Jerusalem were too great to be lamented, so great that they should sink down under them into a silent despair, <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.15-Ezek.24.27">ver. 15-27</reference>.
entries.47ba4d3422dedef01c2410674030190b2ea30ca0: <div eID="gen18881" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18880" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Parable of the Boiling Pot; The Explanation of the Parable. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 590.)</title> <div sID="gen18882" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Again in the ninth year, in the tenth month, in the tenth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Son of man, write thee the name of the day, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of this same day: the king of Babylon set himself against Jerusalem this same day. <hi type="super">3</hi> And utter a parable unto the rebellious house, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Set on a pot, set <hi type="italic">it</hi> on, and also pour water into it: <hi type="super">4</hi> Gather the pieces thereof into it, <hi type="italic">even</hi> every good piece, the thigh, and the shoulder; fill <hi type="italic">it</hi> with the choice bones. <hi type="super">5</hi> Take the choice of the flock, and burn also the bones under it, <hi type="italic">and</hi> make it boil well, and let them seethe the bones of it therein. <hi type="super">6</hi> Wherefore thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Woe to the bloody city, to the pot whose scum <hi type="italic">is</hi> therein, and whose scum is not gone out of it! bring it out piece by piece; let no lot fall upon it. <hi type="super">7</hi> For her blood is in the midst of her; she set it upon the top of a rock; she poured it not upon the ground, to cover it with dust; <hi type="super">8</hi> That it might cause fury to come up to take vengeance; I have set her blood upon the top of a rock, that it should not be covered. <hi type="super">9</hi> Therefore thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Woe to the bloody city! I will even make the pile for fire great. <hi type="super">10</hi> Heap on wood, kindle the fire, consume the flesh, and spice it well, and let the bones be burned. <hi type="super">11</hi> Then set it empty upon the coals thereof, that the brass of it may be hot, and may burn, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> the filthiness of it may be molten in it, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the scum of it may be consumed. <hi type="super">12</hi> She hath wearied <hi type="italic">herself</hi> with lies, and her great scum went not forth out of her: her scum <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> in the fire. <hi type="super">13</hi> In thy filthiness <hi type="italic">is</hi> lewdness: because I have purged thee, and thou wast not purged, thou shalt not be purged from thy filthiness any more, till I have caused my fury to rest upon thee. <hi type="super">14</hi> I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> have spoken <hi type="italic">it:</hi> it shall come to pass, and I will do <hi type="italic">it;</hi> I will not go back, neither will I spare, neither will I repent; according to thy ways, and according to thy doings, shall they judge thee, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <div eID="gen18882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18883" type="x-p"/> We have here, <div eID="gen18883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18884" type="x-p"/> I. The notice God gives to Ezekiel in Babylon of Nebuchadnezzar's laying siege to Jerusalem, just at the time when he was doing it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> take notice, <hi type="italic">the king of Babylon,</hi> who is now abroad with his army, thou knowest not where, <hi type="italic">set himself against Jerusalem this same day.</hi>" It was many miles, it was many days' journey, from Jerusalem to Babylon. Perhaps the last intelligence they had from the army was that the design was upon Rabbath of the children of Ammon and that the campaign was to be opened with the siege of that city. But God knew, and could tell the prophet, "<hi type="italic">This day,</hi> at this time, Jerusalem is invested, and the Chaldean army has sat down before it." Note, As all times, so all places, even the most remote, are present with God and under his view. He tells the prophet, that the prophet might tell the people, that so when it proved to be punctually true, as they would find by the public intelligence in a little time, it might be a confirmation of the prophet's mission, and they might infer that, since he was right in his news, he was so in his predictions, for he owed both to the same correspondence he had with Heaven. <div eID="gen18884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18885" type="x-p"/> II. The notice which he orders him to take of it. He must enter it in his book, <hi type="italic">memorandum,</hi> that <hi type="italic">in the ninth year</hi> of Jehoiachin's captivity (for thence Ezekiel dated, <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.2">ch. i. 2</reference>, which was also the ninth year of Zedekiah's reign, for he began to reign when Jehoiachin was carried off), in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, the king of Babylon laid siege to Jerusalem; and the date here agrees exactly with the date in the history, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.1">2 Kings xxv. 1</reference>. See how God reveals things to his servants the prophets, especially those things which serve to confirm their word, and so to confirm their own faith. Note, It is good to keep an exact account of the date of remarkable occurrences, which may sometimes contribute to the manifesting of God's glory so much the more in them, and the explaining and confirming of scripture prophecies. <hi type="italic">Known unto God are all his works.</hi> <div eID="gen18885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18886" type="x-p"/> III. The notice which he orders him to give to the people thereupon, the purport of which is that this siege of Jerusalem, now begun, will infallibly end in the ruin of it. This he must say <hi type="italic">to the rebellious house,</hi> to those of them that were in Babylon, to be by them communicated to those that were yet in their own land. A rebellious house will soon be a ruinous house. <div eID="gen18886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18887" type="x-p"/> 1. He must show them this by a sign; for that stupid people needed to be taught as children are. The comparison made use of is that of a <hi type="italic">boiling pot.</hi> This agrees with Jeremiah's vision many years before, when he first began to be a prophet, and probably was designed to put them in mind of that (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.13">Jer. i. 13</reference>, <hi type="italic">I see a seething pot, with the face towards the north;</hi> and the explanation of it, <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.15">v. 15</reference>, makes it to signify the besieging of Jerusalem by the <hi type="italic">northern</hi> nations); and, as this comparison is intended to confirm Jeremiah's vision, so also to confront the vain confidence of the princes of Jerusalem, who had said (<reference osisRef="Ezek.11.3">ch. xi. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">This city is the caldron and we are the flesh,</hi> meaning, "We are as safe here as if we were surrounded with walls of brass." "Well," says God, "it shall be so; you shall be boiled in Jerusalem, as the <hi type="italic">flesh in the caldron,</hi> boiled to pieces; let the pot be set on with water in it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.4">v. 4</reference>); let it be filled with the flesh of the <hi type="italic">choice of the flock</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.5">v. 5</reference>), with the choice pieces (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.4">v. 4</reference>), and the marrow-bones, and let the other bones serve for fuel, that, one way or other, either in the pot or under it, the whole beast may be made use of." A fire of bones, though it be a slow fire (for the siege was to be long), is yet a sure and lasting fire; such was God's wrath against them, and not like the <hi type="italic">crackling of thorns under a pot,</hi> which has noise and blaze, but no intense heat. Those that from all parts of the country fled into Jerusalem for safety would be sadly disappointed when the siege laid to it would soon make the place too hot for them; and yet there was not getting out of it, but they must be forced to abide by it, as the flesh in a boiling pot. <div eID="gen18887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18888" type="x-p"/> 2. He must give them a comment upon this sign. It is to be construed as a <hi type="italic">woe to the bloody city,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.6">v. 6</reference>. And again (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.9">v. 9</reference>), being <hi type="italic">bloody,</hi> let it <hi type="italic">go to pot,</hi> to be boiled; that is the fittest place for it. Let us here see, <div eID="gen18888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18889" type="x-p"/> (1.) What is the course God takes with it. Jerusalem, during the siege, is like a pot boiling over the fire, all in a heat, all in a hurry. [1.] Care is taken to keep a good fire under the pot, which signifies the closeness of the siege, and the many vigorous attacks made upon the city by the besiegers, and especially the continued wrath of God burning against them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will make the pile for fire great.</hi> Commission is given to the Chaldeans (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.10">v. 10</reference>) to <hi type="italic">heap on wood, and kindle the fire,</hi> to make Jerusalem more and more hot to the inhabitants. Note, The fire which God kindles for the consuming of impenitent sinners shall never abate, much less go out, for want of fuel. <hi type="italic">Tophet has fire and much wood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Isa. xxx. 33</reference>. [2.] The meat, as it is boiled, is taken out, and given to the Chaldeans for them to feast upon. "<hi type="italic">Consume the flesh;</hi> let it be thoroughly boiled, boiled to rags. <hi type="italic">Spice it well,</hi> and make it savoury, for those that will feast sweetly upon it. <hi type="italic">Let the bones be burnt.</hi>" either the bones <hi type="italic">under</hi> the pot ("let them be consumed with the other fuel") or, as some think, the bones <hi type="italic">in</hi> the pot—"let it boil so furiously that not only the flesh may be sodden, but even the bones softened; let all the inhabitants of Jerusalem be by sickness, sword, and famine, reduced to the extremity of misery." And then (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.6">v. 6</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Bring it out piece by piece;</hi> let every man be delivered into the enemy's hand, to be either put to the sword or made a prisoner. Let them be an easy prey to them, and let the Chaldeans fall upon them as eagerly as a hungry man does upon a good dish of meat when it is set before him. <hi type="italic">Let no lot fall upon it;</hi> every piece in the pot shall be fetched out and devoured, first or last, and therefore it is no matter for casting lots which shall be fetched out first." It was a very severe military execution when David measured Joab with <hi type="italic">two lines to put to death and one full line to keep alive,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">2 Sam. viii. 2</reference>. But here is no line, no lot of mercy, made use of; all goes one way, and that is to destruction. [3.] When all the broth is boiled away the pot is set empty upon the coals, that it may burn too, which signifies the setting of the city on fire, <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.11">v. 11</reference>. The scum of the meat, or (as some translate it) <hi type="italic">the rust of the meat,</hi> has so got into the pot that there is no making it clean by washing or scouring it, and therefore it must be done by fire; so let the filthiness be burnt out of it, or, rather, <hi type="italic">melted in it</hi> and burnt with it. Let the vipers and their nest be consumed together. <div eID="gen18889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18890" type="x-p"/> (2.) What is the quarrel God has with it. He would not take these severe methods with Jerusalem but that he is provoked to it; she deserves to be thus dealt with, for, [1.] It is a bloody city (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.7-Ezek.24.8">v. 7, 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Her blood is in the midst of her.</hi> Many a barbarous murder has been committed in the very heart of the city; nay, and they have a disposition to cruelty in their hearts; they inwardly delight in blood-shed, and so it is <hi type="italic">in the midst of them.</hi> Nay, they commit their murders in the face of the sun, and openly and impudently avow them, in defiance of the justice both of God and man. She did not <hi type="italic">pour out</hi> the blood she shed <hi type="italic">upon the ground, to cover it with dust,</hi> as being ashamed of the sin or afraid of the punishment. She did not look upon it as a filthy thing, proper to be concealed (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.13">Deut. xxiii. 13</reference>), much less dangerous. Nay, she poured out the innocent blood she shed upon a rock, where it would not soak in, upon <hi type="italic">the top of a rock,</hi> in despite of divine views and vengeance. They shed innocent blood under colour of justice; so that they gloried in it, as if they had done God and the country good service, so put it, as it were, <hi type="italic">on the top of a rock.</hi> Or it may refer to the sacrificing of their children on their high places, perhaps on the top of rocks. Now thus they <hi type="italic">caused fury to come up and take vengeance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.8">v. 8</reference>. It could not be avoided but that God <hi type="italic">must</hi> in anger <hi type="italic">visit for these things; his soul must be avenged on such a nation as this.</hi> It is absolutely necessary that such a bloody city as this should have blood given her to drink, for she is worthy, for the vindicating of the honour of divine justice. And, the crime having been public and notorious, it is fit that the punishment should be so too: <hi type="italic">I have set her blood on the top of a rock.</hi> Jerusalem was to be made an example, and therefore was made a spectacle, to the world; God dealt with her according to the law of retaliation. It is fit that those who <hi type="italic">sin before all</hi> should be <hi type="italic">rebuked before all;</hi> and that the reputation of those should not be consulted by the concealment of their punishment who were so impudent as not to desire the concealment of their sin. [2.] It is a filthy city. Great notice is taken, in this explanation of the comparison, of the <hi type="italic">scum of this pot,</hi> which signifies the sin of Jerusalem, working up and appearing when the judgments of God were upon her. It is the pot <hi type="italic">whose scum is therein</hi> and has <hi type="italic">not gone out of it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.6">v. 6</reference>. The <hi type="italic">great scum</hi> that <hi type="italic">went not forth out of her</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.12">v. 12</reference>), that stuck to the pot when all was boiled away, and was <hi type="italic">molten in it</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.11">v. 11</reference>), some of this runs over <hi type="italic">into the fire</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.12">v. 12</reference>), inflames that, and makes it burn the more furiously, but <hi type="italic">it shall all be consumed</hi> at last, <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.11">v. 11</reference>. When the hand of God had gone out against them, instead of humbling themselves under it, repenting and reforming, and accepting the punishment of their iniquity, they grew more impudent and outrageous in sin, quarrelled with God, persecuted his prophets, were fierce to one another, enraged to the last degree against the Chaldeans, snarled at the stone, gnawed their chain, and were like a wild bull in a net. This as <hi type="italic">their scum;</hi> in their distress they <hi type="italic">trespassed yet more against the Lord,</hi> like <hi type="italic">that king Ahaz,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.22">2 Chron. xxviii. 22</reference>. There is little hope of those who are made worse by that which should make them better, whose corruptions are excited an exasperated by those rebukes both of the word and of the providence of God which were designed for the suppressing and subduing of them, or of those whose scum boiled up once in convictions, and confessions of sin, as if it would be taken off by reformation, but afterwards returned again, in a revolt from their good overtures; and the heart that seemed softened is hardened again. This was Jerusalem's case: <hi type="italic">She has wearied with lies,</hi> wearied her God with purposes and promises of amendment, which she never stood to, wearied herself with her carnal confidences, which have all deceived her, <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.12">v. 12</reference>. Note, Those that follow after lying vanities weary themselves with the pursuit. Now see her doom, <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.13-Ezek.24.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. Because she is incurably wicked she is abandoned to ruin, without remedy. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Methods and means of reformation had been tried in vain (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">In thy filthiness is lewdness;</hi> thou hast become obstinate and impudent in it; thou hast got a habit of it, which is confirmed by frequent acts. <hi type="italic">In thy filthiness</hi> there is a rooted lewdness; as appears by this, <hi type="italic">I have purged thee and thou wast not purged.</hi> I have given thee medicine, but it has done thee no good. I have used the means of cleansing thee, but they have been ineffectual; the intention of them has not been answered." Note, It is sad to think how many there are on whom ordinances and providences are all lost. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is therefore resolved that no more such methods shall be used: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not be purged from thy filthiness any more.</hi> The fire shall no longer be a refining fire, but a consuming fire, and therefore shall not be mitigated and shortened, as it has been, but shall be continued in extremity, till it has done its destroying work. Note, Those that will not be healed are justly given up and their case adjudged desperate. There is a day coming when it will be said, <hi type="italic">He that is filthy, let him be filthy still. Thirdly,</hi> Nothing remains then but to bring them to utter ruin: <hi type="italic">I will cause my fury to rest upon thee.</hi> This is the same with what is said of the later Jews, that <hi type="italic">wrath has come upon them to the uttermost,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.16">1 Thess. ii. 16</reference>. They deserve it: <hi type="italic">According to thy doings they shall judge thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.14">v. 14</reference>. And God will do it. The sentence is bound on with repeated ratifications, that they might be awakened to see how certain their ruin was: "<hi type="italic">I the Lord have spoken it,</hi> who am able to make good what I have spoken; <hi type="italic">it shall come to pass,</hi> nothing shall prevent it, for <hi type="italic">I will do it</hi> myself, <hi type="italic">I will not go back</hi> upon any entreaties; the decree has gone forth, and <hi type="italic">I will not spare</hi> in compassion to them, <hi type="italic">neither will I repent.</hi>" He will neither change his mind nor his way. Hereby the prophet was forbidden to interceded for them, and they were forbidden to flatter themselves with hopes of an escape. God hath said it, and he will do it. Note, The declarations of God's wrath against sinners are as inviolable as the assurances he has given of favour to his people; and the case of such is sad indeed, who have brought it to this issue, that either God must be false or they must be damned.
entries.32664f21e97a5fcbef9481dd35bbd2623818998d: <div eID="gen18890" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Death of the Prophet's Wife; A Sign of Jerusalem's Ruin. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 590.)</title> <div sID="gen18891" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Also the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">16</hi> Son of man, behold, I take away from thee the desire of thine eyes with a stroke: yet neither shalt thou mourn nor weep, neither shall thy tears run down. <hi type="super">17</hi> Forbear to cry, make no mourning for the dead, bind the tire of thine head upon thee, and put on thy shoes upon thy feet, and cover not <hi type="italic">thy</hi> lips, and eat not the bread of men. <hi type="super">18</hi> So I spake unto the people in the morning: and at even my wife died; and I did in the morning as I was commanded. <hi type="super">19</hi> And the people said unto me, Wilt thou not tell us what these <hi type="italic">things are</hi> to us, that thou doest <hi type="italic">so?</hi> <hi type="super">20</hi> Then I answered them, The word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">21</hi> Speak unto the house of Israel, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Behold, I will profane my sanctuary, the excellency of your strength, the desire of your eyes, and that which your soul pitieth; and your sons and your daughters whom ye have left shall fall by the sword. <hi type="super">22</hi> And ye shall do as I have done: ye shall not cover <hi type="italic">your</hi> lips, nor eat the bread of men. <hi type="super">23</hi> And your tires <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> upon your heads, and your shoes upon your feet: ye shall not mourn nor weep; but ye shall pine away for your iniquities, and mourn one toward another. <hi type="super">24</hi> Thus Ezekiel is unto you a sign: according to all that he hath done shall ye do: and when this cometh, ye shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <hi type="super">25</hi> Also, thou son of man, <hi type="italic">shall it</hi> not <hi type="italic">be</hi> in the day when I take from them their strength, the joy of their glory, the desire of their eyes, and that whereupon they set their minds, their sons and their daughters, <hi type="super">26</hi> <hi type="italic">That</hi> he that escapeth in that day shall come unto thee, to cause <hi type="italic">thee</hi> to hear <hi type="italic">it</hi> with <hi type="italic">thine</hi> ears? <hi type="super">27</hi> In that day shall thy mouth be opened to him which is escaped, and thou shalt speak, and be no more dumb: and thou shalt be a sign unto them; and they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen18891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18892" type="x-p"/> These verses conclude what we have been upon all along from the beginning of this book, to wit, Ezekiel's prophecies of the destruction of Jerusalem; for after this, though he prophesied much concerning other nations, he said no more concerning Jerusalem, till he heard of the destruction of it, almost three years after, <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.21">ch. xxxiii. 21</reference>. He had assured them, in the former part of this chapter, that there was no hope at all of the preventing of the trouble; here he assures them that they should not have the ease of weeping for it. Observe here, <div eID="gen18892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18893" type="x-p"/> I. The sign by which this was represented to them, and it was a sign that cost the prophet very dear; the more shame for them that when he, by a divine appointment, was at such an expense to affect them with what he had to deliver, yet they were not affected by it. <div eID="gen18893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18894" type="x-p"/> 1. He must lose a good wife, that should suddenly be taken from him by death. God gave him notice of it before, that it might be the less surprise to him (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold, I take away from thee the desire of thy eyes with a stroke.</hi> Note, (1.) A married state may very well agree with the prophetical office; it is <hi type="italic">honourable in all,</hi> and therefore not sinful in ministers. (2.) Much of the comfort of human life lies in agreeable relations. No doubt Ezekiel found a prudent tender yoke-fellow, that shared with him in his griefs and cares, to be a happy companion in his captivity. (3.) Those in the conjugal relation must be to each other not only a <hi type="italic">covering of the eyes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.20.16">Gen. xx. 16</reference>), to restrain wandering looks after others; but a <hi type="italic">desire of the eyes,</hi> to engage pleasing looks on one another. A beloved wife is the <hi type="italic">desire of the eyes,</hi> which find not any object more grateful. (4.) That is least safe which is most dear; we know not how soon the desire of our eyes may be removed from us and may become the sorrow of our hearts, which is a good reason why those that <hi type="italic">have wives</hi> should be <hi type="italic">as though they had none,</hi> and those <hi type="italic">who rejoice</hi> in them <hi type="italic">as though they rejoiced not,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.29-1Cor.7.30">1 Cor. vii. 29, 30</reference>. Death is a stroke which the most pious, the most useful, the most amiable, are not exempted from. (5.) When the desire of our eyes is taken away with a stroke we must see and own the hand of God in it: <hi type="italic">I take away the desire of thy eyes.</hi> He takes our creature-comforts from us when and how he pleases; he gave them to us, but reserved to himself a property in them; and <hi type="italic">may he not do what he will with his own?</hi> (6.) Under afflictions of this kind it is good for us to remember that we are <hi type="italic">sons of men;</hi> for so God calls the prophet here. If thou art a <hi type="italic">son of Adam,</hi> thy wife is a daughter of <hi type="italic">Eve,</hi> and therefore a dying creature. It is an affliction which the children of men are liable to; and <hi type="italic">shall the earth be forsaken for us?</hi> According to this prediction, he tells us (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.18">v. 18</reference>), <hi type="italic">I spoke unto the people in the morning;</hi> for God sent his prophets, <hi type="italic">rising up early</hi> and sending them; then he thought, if ever, they would be disposed to hearken to him. Observe, [1.] Though God had given Ezekiel a certain prospect of this affliction coming upon him, yet it did not take him off from his work, but he resolved to go on in that. [2.] We may the more easily bear an affliction if it find us in the way of our duty; for nothing can hurt us, nothing come amiss to us, while we keep ourselves in the love of God. <div eID="gen18894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18895" type="x-p"/> 2. He must deny himself the satisfaction of mourning for his wife, which would have been both an honour to her and an ease to the oppression of his own spirit. He must not use the natural expressions of sorrow, <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.16">v. 16</reference>. He must not give vent to his passion by <hi type="italic">weeping,</hi> or letting <hi type="italic">his tears run down,</hi> though tears are a tribute due to the dead, and, when the body is sown, it is fit that it should thus be watered. But Ezekiel is not allowed to do this, though he thought he had as much reason to do it as any man and would perhaps be ill thought of by the people if he did it not. Much less might he use the customary formalities of mourners. He must dress himself in his usual attire, must bind his turban on him, here called the <hi type="italic">tire of his head,</hi> must <hi type="italic">put on his shoes,</hi> and not go barefoot, as was usual in such cases; he must not <hi type="italic">cover his lips,</hi> not throw a veil over his face (as mourners were wont to do, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.45">Lev. xiii. 45</reference>), must not be of a <hi type="italic">sorrowful countenance, appearing unto men to fast,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.6.18">Matt. vi. 18</reference>. He must not <hi type="italic">eat the bread of men,</hi> nor expect that his neighbours and friends should send him in provisions, as usually they did in such cases, presuming the mourners had no heart to provide meat for themselves; but, if it were sent, he must not eat of it, but go on in his business as at other times. It could not but be greatly against the grain to flesh and blood not to lament the death of one he loved so dearly, but so God commands; and <hi type="italic">I did in the morning as I was commanded.</hi> He appeared in public, in his usual habit, and looked as he used to do, without any signs of mourning. (1.) Here there was something peculiar, and Ezekiel, to make himself a sign to the people, must put a force upon himself and exercise an extraordinary piece of self-denial. Note, Our dispositions must always submit to God's directions, and his command must be obeyed even in that which is most difficult and displeasing to us. (2.) Though mourning for the dead be a duty, yet it must always be kept under the government of religion and right reason, and we must not <hi type="italic">sorrow as those that have no hope,</hi> nor lament the loss of any creature, even the most valuable, and that which we could worst spare, as if we had lost our God, or as if all our happiness were gone with it; and, of this moderation in mourning, ministers, when it is their case, ought to be examples. We must at such a time study to improve the affliction, to accommodate ourselves to it, and to get our acquaintance with the other world increased, by the removal of our dear relations, and learn with holy Job <hi type="italic">to bless the name of the Lord</hi> even when he takes as well as when he gives. <div eID="gen18895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18896" type="x-p"/> II. The explication and application of this sign. The people enquired the meaning of it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wilt thou not tell us what these things are to us that thou doest so?</hi> They knew that Ezekiel was an affectionate husband, that the death of his wife was a great affliction to him, and that he would not appear so unconcerned at it but for some good reason and for instruction to them; and perhaps they were in hopes that it had a favourable signification, and gave them an intimation that God would now comfort them again according to the time he had afflicted them, and make them look pleasant again. Note, When we are enquiring concerning the things of God our enquiry must be, "What are those thing <hi type="italic">to us?</hi> What are we concerned in them? What conviction, what counsel, what comfort, do they speak to us? Wherein do they reach our case?" Ezekiel gives them an answer <hi type="italic">verbatim—word for word</hi> as he had received it from the Lord, who had told him what he must <hi type="italic">speak to the house of Israel.</hi> <div eID="gen18896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18897" type="x-p"/> 1. Let them know that as Ezekiel's wife was taken from him by a stroke so would God take from them all that which was dearest to them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.21">v. 21</reference>. If this was <hi type="italic">done to the green tree, what shall be done to the dry?</hi> If a faithful servant of God was thus afflicted only for his trial, shall such a generation of rebels against God go unpunished? By this awakening providence God showed that he was in earnest in his threatenings, and inexorable. We may suppose that Ezekiel prayed that, if it were the will of God, his wife might be spared to him, but God would not hear him; and should he be heard then in his intercessions for this provoking people? No, it is determined: <hi type="italic">God will take away the desire of your eyes.</hi> Note, The removal of the comforts of others should awaken us to think of parting with ours too; for <hi type="italic">are we better than they?</hi> We know not how soon the same cup, or a more bitter one, may be put into our hands, and should therefore weep with those that weep, as being ourselves also in the body. God will <hi type="italic">take away that which their soul pities,</hi> that is, of which they say, What a pity is it that it should be cut off and destroyed! That <hi type="italic">for which your souls are afraid</hi> (so some read it); you shall lose that which you most dread the loss of. And what is that? (1.) That which was their public pride, the temple: "<hi type="italic">I will profane my sanctuary,</hi> by giving that into the enemy's hand, to be plundered and burnt." This was signified by the death of a wife, a dear wife, to teach us that God's sanctuary should be dearer to us, and more <hi type="italic">the desire of our eyes,</hi> than any creature-comfort whatsoever. Christ's church, that is his spouse, should be ours too. Though this people were very corrupt, and had themselves profaned the sanctuary, yet it is called <hi type="italic">the desire of their eyes.</hi> Note, Many that are destitute of <hi type="italic">the power of godliness</hi> are yet very fond of <hi type="italic">the form</hi> of it; and it is just with God to punish them for their hypocrisy by depriving them of that too. The sanctuary is here called the <hi type="italic">excellency of their strength;</hi> they had many strong-holds and places of defence, but the temple excelled them all. It was the <hi type="italic">pride of their strength;</hi> they prided in it as their strength that they were <hi type="italic">the temple of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.7.4">Jer. vii. 4</reference>. Note, The church-privileges that men are proud of are profaned by their sins, and it is just with God to profane them by his judgments. And with these God will take away, (2.) That which was their family-pleasure, which they looked upon with delight: "<hi type="italic">Your sons and your daughters</hi> (which are the dearer to you because they are but few left of many, the rest having perished by famine and pestilence) shall <hi type="italic">fall by the sword</hi> of the Chaldeans." What a dreadful spectacle would it be to see their own children, pieces, pictures, of themselves, whom they had taken such care and pains to bring up, and whom they loved as their own souls, sacrificed to the rage of the merciless conquerors! This, this, was the punishment of sin. <div eID="gen18897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18898" type="x-p"/> 2. Let them know that as Ezekiel wept not for his affliction so neither should they weep for theirs. He must say, <hi type="italic">You shall do as I have done,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.22">v. 22</reference>. <hi type="italic">You shall not mourn nor weep,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.23">v. 23</reference>. Jeremiah had told them the same, that men <hi type="italic">shall not lament for the dead nor cut themselves</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.6">Jer. xvi. 6</reference>); not that there shall be any such merciful circumstance without, or any such degrees of wisdom and grace within, as shall mitigate and moderate the sorrow; but they <hi type="italic">shall not mourn,</hi> for, (1.) Their grief shall be so great that they shall be quite overwhelmed with it; their passions shall stifle them, and they shall have no power to ease themselves by giving vent to it. (2.) Their calamities shall come so fast upon them, one upon the neck of another, that by long custom they shall be <hi type="italic">hardened in their sorrows</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.6.10">Job vi. 10</reference>) and perfectly stupefied, and moped (as we say), with them. (3.) They shall not dare to express their grief, for fear of being deemed disaffected to the conquerors, who would take their lamentations as an affront and disturbance to their triumphs. (4.) They shall not have hearts, nor time, nor money, wherewith to put themselves in mourning, and accommodate themselves with the ceremonies of grief: "You will be so entirely taken up with solid substantial grief that you will have no room for the shadow of it." (5.) Particular mourners shall not need to distinguish themselves by <hi type="italic">covering their lips,</hi> and laying aside their ornaments, and <hi type="italic">going barefoot;</hi> for it is well known that every body is a mourner. (6.) There shall be none of that sense of their affliction and sorrow for it which would help to bring them to repentance, but that only which shall drive them to despair; so it follows: "<hi type="italic">You shall pine away for your iniquities,</hi> with seared consciences and reprobate minds, and <hi type="italic">you shall mourn,</hi> not to God in prayer and confession of sin, but <hi type="italic">one towards another,</hi>" murmuring, and fretting, and complaining of God, thus making their burden heavier and their wound more grievous, as impatient people do under their afflictions by mingling their own passions with them. <div eID="gen18898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18899" type="x-p"/> III. An appeal to the event, for the confirmation of all this (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.24">v. 24</reference>): "<hi type="italic">When this comes,</hi> as it is foretold, when Jerusalem, which is this day besieged, is quite destroyed and laid waste, which now you cannot believe will ever be, <hi type="italic">then you shall know that I am the Lord God,</hi> who have given you this fair warning of it. Then you will remember that Ezekiel was to you a sign." Note, Those who regard not the threatenings of the word when they are preached will be made to remember them when they are executed. Observe, <div eID="gen18899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18900" type="x-p"/> 1. The great desolation which the siege of Jerusalem should end in (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">In that day,</hi> that terrible day, when the city shall be broken up, <hi type="italic">I will take from them,</hi> (1.) That which they depended on—<hi type="italic">their strength,</hi> their walls, their treasures, their fortifications, their men of war; none shall stand them in stead. (2.) That which they boasted of—the <hi type="italic">joy of their glory,</hi> that which they looked upon as most their glory, and which they most rejoiced in, the temple of their God and the palaces of their princes. (3.) That which they delighted in, which was the <hi type="italic">desire of their eyes,</hi> and on which they <hi type="italic">set their minds.</hi> Note, Carnal people set their minds upon that on which they can set their eyes; they look at, and dote upon, <hi type="italic">the things that are seen;</hi> and it is their folly to <hi type="italic">set their minds</hi> upon that which they have no assurance of and which may be taken from them in a moment, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.5">Prov. xxiii. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Their sons and their daughters</hi> were all this—<hi type="italic">their strength, and joy, and glory;</hi> and these shall go into captivity. <div eID="gen18900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18901" type="x-p"/> 2. The notice that should be brought to the prophet, not be revelation, as the notice of the siege was brought to him (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.2">v. 2</reference>), but in an ordinary way (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.26">v. 26</reference>): "<hi type="italic">He that escapes in that day</hi> shall, by a special direction of Providence, <hi type="italic">come to thee,</hi> to bring thee intelligence of it," which we find was done, <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.21">ch. xxxiii. 21</reference>. The ill-news came slowly, and yet to Ezekiel and his fellow-captives it came too soon. <div eID="gen18901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18902" type="x-p"/> 3. The divine impression which he should be under upon receiving that notice, <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.27">v. 27</reference>. Whereas, from this time to that, Ezekiel was thus far dumb that he prophesied no more against the land of Israel, but against the neighbouring nations, as we shall find in the following chapters, then he shall have orders given him to <hi type="italic">speak again to the children of his people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.33.2">ch. xxxiii. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.22">22</reference>); then <hi type="italic">his mouth shall be opened.</hi> He was suspended from prophesying against them in the mean time, because, Jerusalem being besieged, his prophecies could not be sent into the city,—because, when God was speaking so loudly by the rod, there was the less need of speaking by the word,—and because then the accomplishment of his prophecies would be the full confirmation of his mission, and would the more effectually clear the way for him to begin again. It being referred to that issue, that issue must be waited for. Thus Christ forbade his disciples to preach openly that he was Christ till after his resurrection, because that was to be the full proof of it. "But then <hi type="italic">thou shalt speak</hi> with the greater assurance, and the more effectually, either to their conviction or to their confusion." Note, God's prophets are never silenced but for wise and holy ends. And when God gives them the opening of the mouth again (as he will in due time, for even the witnesses that are <hi type="italic">slain</hi> shall <hi type="italic">arise</hi>) it shall appear to have been for his glory that they were for a while silent, that people may the more certainly and fully <hi type="italic">know</hi> that <hi type="italic">God is the Lord.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ezek.24"/> <div eID="gen18902" type="x-p"/>

entries.f3fd3cd99a1d32949c7aaf229442087721f4ba85: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11462"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 24</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.24.1-Ezek.24.27">Eze 24:1-27</reference>. Vision of the Boiling Caldron, and of the Death of Ezekiel's Wife.</title> <div sID="gen20742" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11462"/>1-2. Ezekiel proves his divine mission by announcing the very day, ("this same day") of the beginning of the investment of the city by Nebuchadnezzar; "the ninth year," namely, of Jehoiachin's captivity, "the tenth day of the tenth month"; though he was three hundred miles away from Jerusalem among the captives at the Chebar (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.1">2Ki 25:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.39.1">Jr 39:1</reference>). <div eID="gen20742" type="x-p"/>
entries.854e9f4a771fe569fb3b9949520c2855193addc6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11464"/><div sID="gen20744" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11464"/><hi type="bold">3. pot--</hi>caldron. Alluding to the self-confident proverb used among the people, <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.3">Eze 11:3</reference> (see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.3">Eze 11:3</reference>), "This city is the caldron and we be the flesh"; your proverb shall prove awfully true, but in a different sense from what you intend. So far from the city proving an iron, caldron-like defense from the fire, it shall be as a caldron set on the fire, and the people as so many pieces of meat subjected to boiling heat. See <reference osisRef="Jer.1.13">Jr 1:13</reference>. <div eID="gen20744" type="x-p"/>
entries.a777148287631abf592a566896eb67aa842ed082: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11465"/><div sID="gen20745" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11465"/><hi type="bold">4. pieces thereof--</hi>those which properly belong to it, as its own.<div eID="gen20745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20746" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every good piece ... choice bones--</hi>that is, the most distinguished of the people. The "choice bones" in the pot have flesh adhering to them. The bones under the pot (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.5">Eze 24:5</reference>) are those having no flesh and used as fuel, answering to the poorest who suffer first, and are put out of pain sooner than the rich who endure what answers to the slower process of boiling. <div eID="gen20746" type="x-p"/>
entries.71103c587432db51d08bb784d9c465b7a0e1558e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11466"/><div sID="gen20747" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11466"/><hi type="bold">5. burn ... bones--</hi>rather, "pile the bones." Literally, "Let there be a round pile of the bones."<div eID="gen20747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20748" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therein--</hi>literally, "in the midst of it." <div eID="gen20748" type="x-p"/>
entries.c3c0660ff88d297c0cdb18a77d578c0f0b4ec398: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11467"/><div sID="gen20749" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11467"/><hi type="bold">6. scum--</hi>not ordinary, but poisonous scum, that is, the people's all-pervading wickedness.<div eID="gen20749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20750" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring it out piece by piece--</hi>"it," the contents of the pot; its flesh, that is, "I will destroy the people of the city, not all at the same time, but by a series of successive attacks." Not as Fairbairn, "on its every piece let it (the poisonous scum) go forth."<div eID="gen20750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20751" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let no lot fall upon it--</hi>that is, no lot, such as is sometimes cast, to decide who are to be destroyed and who saved (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">2Sa 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.3">Joe 3:3</reference>; Ob 11; <reference osisRef="Nah.3.10">Na 3:10</reference>). In former carryings away of captives, lots were cast to settle who were to go, and who to stay, but now all alike are to be cast out without distinction of rank, age, or sex. <div eID="gen20751" type="x-p"/>
entries.1e0e4fe4a91c5047888e5cab5880a95413b123b9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11468"/><div sID="gen20752" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11468"/><hi type="bold">7. upon the top of a rock--</hi>or, "the dry, bare, exposed rock," so as to be conspicuous to all. Blood poured on a rock is not so soon absorbed as blood poured on the earth. The law ordered the blood even of a beast or fowl to be "covered with the dust" (<reference osisRef="Lev.17.13">Le 17:13</reference>); but Jerusalem was so shameless as to be at no pains to cover up the blood of innocent men slain in her. Blood, as the consummation of all sin, presupposes every other form of guilt. <div eID="gen20752" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d77dc8235582e3a419e4e03af186d431d4ebf80: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11469"/><div sID="gen20753" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11469"/><hi type="bold">8. That it might cause--</hi>God purposely let her so shamelessly pour the blood on the bare rock, "that it might" the more loudly and openly cry for vengeance from on high; and that the connection between the guilt and the punishment might be the more palpable. The blood of Abel, though the ground received it, still cries to heaven for vengeance (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.10">Ge 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.4.11">11</reference>); much more blood shamelessly exposed on the bare rock.<div eID="gen20753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20754" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set her blood--</hi>She shall be paid back in kind (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.2">Mt 7:2</reference>). She openly shed blood, and her blood shall openly be shed. <div eID="gen20754" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e49fc4073e18b7e89606f9fb0144295def381f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11470"/><div sID="gen20755" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11470"/><hi type="bold">9. the pile for fire--</hi>the hostile materials for the city's destruction. <div eID="gen20755" type="x-p"/>
entries.63e06540189f897d08003fad0fcb781af13eb9e9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11471"/><div sID="gen20756" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11471"/><hi type="bold">10. spice it well--</hi>that the meat may be the more palatable, that is, I will make the foe delight in its destruction as much as one delights in well-seasoned, savory meat. Grotius, needlessly departing from the obvious sense, translates, "Let it be boiled down to a compound." <div eID="gen20756" type="x-p"/>
entries.98da9edef60f67ed081ec4811758efc2dffbff8a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11472"/><div sID="gen20757" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11472"/><hi type="bold">11. set it empty ... that ... brass ... may burn, ... that ... scum ... may be consumed--</hi>Even the consumption of the contents is not enough; the caldron itself which is infected by the poisonous scum must be destroyed, that is, the city itself must be destroyed, not merely the inhabitants, just as the very house infected with leprosy was to be destroyed (<reference osisRef="Lev.14.34-Lev.14.45">Le 14:34-45</reference>). <div eID="gen20757" type="x-p"/>
entries.9cd5a679c1ee4500bacee876d4ac62bd53995aa6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11473"/><div sID="gen20758" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11473"/><hi type="bold">12. herself--</hi>rather, "she hath wearied Me out with lies"; or rather, "with vain labors" on My part to purify her without being obliged to have recourse to judgments (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.43.24">Is 43:24</reference>; Mal 2:17) [Maurer]. However, English Version gives a good sense (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.47.13">Is 47:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.10">57:10</reference>). <div eID="gen20758" type="x-p"/>
entries.55f30f97e1614ecd2eb4a0b3d3fb005ddb3fb6d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11474"/><div sID="gen20759" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11474"/><hi type="bold">13. lewdness--</hi>determined, deliberate wickedness; from a Hebrew root, "to purpose."<div eID="gen20759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20760" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I have purged thee--</hi>that is, I have left nothing untried which would tend towards purging thee, by sending prophets to invite thee to repentance, by giving thee the law with all its promises, privileges, and threats.<div eID="gen20760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20761" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou shalt not be purged ... any more--</hi>that is, by My gracious interpositions; thou shalt be left to thine own course to take its fatal consequences. <div eID="gen20761" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f9c9d07d30e18c0f5347a9255b93cf70e58a7b5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11475"/><div sID="gen20762" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11475"/><hi type="bold">14. go back--</hi>desist; relax [Fairbairn]. <div eID="gen20762" type="x-p"/>
entries.4b3d55f30234424df855851766b28a7273a7a5d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11476"/><div sID="gen20763" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11476"/>15. Second part of the vision; announcement of the death of Ezekiel's wife, and prohibition of the usual signs of mourning. <div eID="gen20763" type="x-p"/>
entries.f078916087ff18373892269e6a0cb1891112394b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11477"/><div sID="gen20764" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11477"/><hi type="bold">16. desire of ... eyes--</hi>his wife: representing the sanctuary (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.21">Eze 24:21</reference>) in which the Jews so much gloried. The energy and subordination of Ezekiel's whole life to his prophetic office is strikingly displayed in this narrative of his wife's death. It is the only memorable event of his personal history which he records, and this only in reference to his soul-absorbing work. His natural tenderness is shown by that graphic touch, "the desire of thine eyes." What amazing subjection, then, of his individual feeling to his prophetic duty is manifested in the simple statement (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.18">Eze 24:18</reference>), "So I spake ... in the morning; and at even my wife died; and I did in the morning as I was commanded."<div eID="gen20764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stroke--</hi>a sudden visitation. The suddenness of it enhances the self-control of Ezekiel in so entirely merging individual feeling, which must have been especially acute under such trying circumstances, in the higher claims of duty to God. <div eID="gen20765" type="x-p"/>
entries.c632f9171b850d49f7ab1f9547c4e0efadfadc2c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11478"/><div sID="gen20766" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11478"/><hi type="bold">17. Forbear to cry--</hi>or, "Lament in silence"; not forbidding sorrow, but the loud expression of it [Grotius].<div eID="gen20766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20767" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no mourning--</hi>typical of the universality of the ruin of Jerusalem, which would preclude mourning, such as is usual where calamity is but partial. "The dead" is purposely put in the plural, as referring ultimately to the dead who should perish at the taking of Jerusalem; though the singular might have been expected, as Ezekiel's wife was the immediate subject referred to: "make no mourning," such as is usual, "for the dead, and such as shall be hereafter in Jerusalem" (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.5-Jer.16.7">Jr 16:5-7</reference>).<div eID="gen20767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20768" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tire of thine head--</hi>thy headdress [Fairbairn]. Jerome explains, "Thou shalt retain the hair which is usually cut in mourning." The fillet, binding the hair about the temples like a chaplet, was laid aside at such times. Uncovering the head was an ordinary sign of mourning in priests; whereas others covered their heads in mourning (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">2Sa 15:30</reference>). The reason was, the priests had their headdress of fine twined linen given them for ornament, and as a badge of office. The high priest, as having on his head the holy anointing oil, was forbidden in any case to lay aside his headdress. But the priests might do so in the case of the death of the nearest relatives (<reference osisRef="Lev.21.2">Le 21:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.3.10">3, 10</reference>). They then put on inferior attire, sprinkling also on their heads dust and ashes (compare <reference osisRef="Lev.10.6">Le 10:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.10.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen20768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shoes upon thy feet--</hi>whereas mourners went "barefoot" (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">2Sa 15:30</reference>).<div eID="gen20769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20770" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cover not ... lips--</hi>rather, the "upper lip," with the moustache (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.45">Le 13:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.3.7">Mi 3:7</reference>).<div eID="gen20770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20771" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bread of men--</hi>the bread usually brought to mourners by friends in token of sympathy. So the "cup of consolation" brought (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.7">Jr 16:7</reference>). "Of men" means such as is usually furnished by men. So <reference osisRef="Isa.8.1">Is 8:1</reference>, "a man's pen"; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.17">Re 21:17</reference>, "the measure of a man." <div eID="gen20771" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b86d2e4e0d3ff40dfb60cb25fc067ae966ecd80: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11479"/><div sID="gen20772" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11479"/><hi type="bold">19. what these things are to us--</hi>The people perceive that Ezekiel's strange conduct has a symbolical meaning as to themselves; they ask, "What is that meaning?" <div eID="gen20772" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9459c04498bde4ac402b0989054b647c9e7664c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11480"/><div sID="gen20773" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11480"/><hi type="bold">21. excellency of your strength--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Amos.6.8">Am 6:8</reference>). The object of your pride and confidence (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.4">Jr 7:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.14">10, 14</reference>).<div eID="gen20773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20774" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">desire of ... eyes--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.27.4">Psa 27:4</reference>). The antitype to Ezekiel's wife (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.16">Eze 24:16</reference>).<div eID="gen20774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20775" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pitieth--</hi>loveth, as pity is akin to love: "yearned over."<div eID="gen20775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20776" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Profane--</hi>an appropriate word. They had profaned the temple with idolatry; God, in just retribution, will profane it with the Chaldean sword, that is, lay it in the dust, as Ezekiel's wife.<div eID="gen20776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20777" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sons ... daughters ... left--</hi>the children left behind in Judea, when the parents were carried away. <div eID="gen20777" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6ae6a781c73f47a118d70b1fc9e026bc57deeb2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11481"/><div sID="gen20778" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11481"/>22. (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.6">Jr 16:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.7">7</reference>). So general shall be the calamity, that all ordinary usages of mourning shall be suspended. <div eID="gen20778" type="x-p"/>
entries.4ec810fa99f43e33b192e58c77c08a915873c0cc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11482"/><div sID="gen20779" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11482"/><hi type="bold">23. ye shall not mourn ... but ... pine away for your iniquities--</hi>The Jews' not mourning was to be not the result of insensibility, any more than Ezekiel's not mourning for his wife was not from want of feeling. They could not in their exile manifest publicly their lamentation, but they would privately "mourn one to another." Their "iniquities" would then be their chief sorrow ("pining away"), as feeling that these were the cause of their sufferings (compare <reference osisRef="Lev.26.39">Le 26:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.39">La 3:39</reference>). The fullest fulfilment is still future (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.10-Zech.12.14">Zec 12:10-14</reference>). <div eID="gen20779" type="x-p"/>
entries.9f48c5b3aafc8d78b6a89592c7a57a9966736600: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11483"/><div sID="gen20780" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11483"/><hi type="bold">24. sign--</hi>a typical representative in his own person of what was to befall them (<reference osisRef="Isa.20.3">Is 20:3</reference>).<div eID="gen20780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20781" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when this cometh--</hi>alluding probably to their taunt, as if God's word spoken by His prophets would never come to pass. "Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come now" (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.15">Jr 17:15</reference>). When the prophecy is fulfilled, "ye shall know (to your cost) that I am the Lord," who thereby show My power and fulfil My word spoken by My prophet (<reference osisRef="John.13.19">Joh 13:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.29">14:29</reference>). <div eID="gen20781" type="x-p"/>
entries.4eecbb5c7c9f0da168afe56b2833a8b68a944ca2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11484"/><div sID="gen20782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11484"/>25-26. "The day" referred to in these verses is the day of the overthrow of the temple, when the fugitive "escapes." But "that day," in <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.27">Eze 24:27</reference>, is the day on which the fugitive brings the sad news to Ezekiel, at the Chebar. In the interval the prophet suspended his prophecies as to the Jews, as was foretold. Afterwards his mouth was "opened," and no more "dumb" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.3.26">Eze 3:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.27">27</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.27">Eze 24:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.21">33:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.22">22</reference>). <chapter eID="Ezek.24"/>

entries.14e6ab79b43a43a0b113271fa51d7c949f8dd7ce: <div eID="gen31919" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen31920" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31921" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31921" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31920" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31922" type="x-p"/> The prophet now informs those of the captivity of the very day on which Nebuchadnezzar was to lay siege to Jerusalem, (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.52.4">Jer 52:4</reference>), and describes the fate of that city and its inhabitants by a very apt similitude, <reference osisRef="Eze.24.1-Eze.24.14">Eze 24:1-14</reference>. As another sign of the greatness of those calamities the prophet is forbidden to mourn for his wife, of whom he is to be deprived; intimating thereby that the sufferings of the Jews should be so astonishing as to surpass all expressions of grief; and that private sorrow however affectionate and tender the object, ought to be absorbed in the public calamities, <reference osisRef="Eze.24.15-Eze.24.18">Eze 24:15-18</reference>. The prophet, having farther expressed his prediction in plain terms, intimates that he was to speak to them no more till they should have the news of these prophecies having been fulfilled, <reference osisRef="Eze.24.19-Eze.24.27">Eze 24:19-27</reference>. <div eID="gen31922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31923" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen31923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31924" type="x-p"/> The ninth year - This prophecy was given in the ninth year of Zedekiah, about Thursday, the thirtieth of January, A.M. 3414; the very day in which the king of Babylon commenced the siege of Jerusalem.
entries.027e50d62314e925dd3f99f793e6e26f87edfd15: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen31924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31925" type="x-p"/> Set on a pot - The pot was Jerusalem; the flesh, the inhabitants in general; every good piece, the thigh and the shoulder, King Zedekiah and his family; the bones, the soldiers; and the setting on the pot, the commencement of the siege. The prophet was then in Mesopotamia; and he was told particularly to mark the day, etc., that it might be seen how precisely the spirit of prophecy had shown the very day in which the siege took place. Under the same image of a boiling pot, Jeremiah had represented the siege of Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Jer.1.13">Jer 1:13</reference>. Ezekiel was a priest; the action of boiling pots was familiar to him, as these things were much in use in the temple service.
entries.155312dbd945a56d5dd37e72af8baa60dc636f75: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen31925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31926" type="x-p"/> Make it boil well - Let it boil over, that its own scum may augment the fire, that the bones - the soldiers, may be seethed therein. Let its contentions, divided counsels, and disunion be the means of increasing its miseries, רתח רתחיה rattach rethacheyha, let it bubble its bubbling; something like that of the poet: - "Bubble, bubble, toil and trouble: <div eID="gen31926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31927" type="x-p"/> Fire burn, and cauldron bubble." <div eID="gen31927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31928" type="x-p"/> Very like the noise made by ebullition, when a pot of thick broth, "sleek and slab," is set over a fierce fire. Such was that here represented in which all the flesh, the fat and the bones were to be boiled, and generally dissolved together.
entries.6295aa61ca4a15818b4907ca11cb4600a7095b31: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen31928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31929" type="x-p"/> Let no lot fall upon it - Pull out the flesh indiscriminately; let no piece be chosen for king or priest; thus showing that all should be involved in one indiscriminate ruin.
entries.33e97fec688d4c19205a8e2879142d3e2357fb53: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen31929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31930" type="x-p"/> For her blood is in the midst of her - She gloried in her idol sacrifices; she offered them upon a rock, where the blood should remain evident; and she poured none upon the ground to cover it with dust, in horror of that moral evil that required the blood of an innocent creature to be shed, in order to the atonement of the offender's guilt. To "cover the blood of the victim," was a command of the law, <reference osisRef="Lev.17.13">Lev 17:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.12.24">Deu 12:24</reference>.
entries.37dbe117a58c399a5ae8e3621dbb6b3a7001c5a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen31930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31931" type="x-p"/> That it might cause fury - This very blood shall be against them, as the blood of Abel was against Cain.
entries.4469b0a156141f14b2c7135f5e26aad9460ed7dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen31931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31932" type="x-p"/> Heap or wood - Let the siege be severe, the carnage great, and the ruin and catastrophe complete.
entries.cbd24d4337c2e984b6e9875fcb262b464d5fb820: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen31932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31933" type="x-p"/> In thy filthiness is lewdness - זמה zimmah, a word that denominates the worst kinds of impurity; adultery, incest, etc., and the purpose, wish, design, and ardent desire to do these things. Hers were not accidental sins, they were abominations by design, and they were the worse in her, because God had cleansed her, had separated the Israelites from idolatry and idolatrous nations, and by his institutions removed from them all idolatrous incentives. But they formed alliances with the heathen, and adopted all their abominations; therefore God would not spare them. See <reference osisRef="Eze.24.14">Eze 24:14</reference>.
entries.d135997cadca52754684e1df3a088eacc03078de: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen31933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31934" type="x-p"/> Behold, I take away from thee the desire of thine eyes - Here is an intimation that the stroke he was to suffer was to be above all grief; that it would be so great as to prevent the relief of tears. <div eID="gen31934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31935" type="x-p"/> Curae leves loquuntur, graviores silent, is a well-accredited maxim in such cases. Superficial griefs affect the more easily moved passions; great ones affect the soul itself, in its powers of reasoning, reflecting, comparing, recollecting, etc., when the sufferer feels all the weight of wo. <div eID="gen31935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31936" type="x-p"/> Neither shall thy tears run down - Τουτο γαρ ιδιον των οφθαλμων εν τοις μεγαλοις κακοις· εν μεν γαρ ταις μετριαις συμφοραις αφθονως τα δακρυα καταρῥει, - εν δε τοις ὑπερβαλλουσι δεινοις φευγει και τα δακρυα και προδιδωσι και τους αφθαλμους· Achill. Tat. lib. 3. c. 11. For this is the case with the eyes in great calamities: in light misfortunes tears flow freely, but in heavy afflictions tears fly away, and betray the eyes.
entries.89af5698e5127885064bb45b16d08d59c8ca1f00: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen31936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31937" type="x-p"/> Make no mourning - As a priest, he could make no public mourning, <reference osisRef="Lev.21.1">Lev 21:1</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen31937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31938" type="x-p"/> Bind the tire of thine head - This seems to refer to the high priest's bonnet; or perhaps, one worn by the ordinary priests: it might have been a black veil to cover the head. <div eID="gen31938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31939" type="x-p"/> Put on thy shoes upon thy feet - Walking barefoot was a sign of grief. <div eID="gen31939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31940" type="x-p"/> Cover not thy lips - Mourners covered the under part of the face, from the nose to the bottom of the chin. <div eID="gen31940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31941" type="x-p"/> Eat not the bread of men - לחם אנשים lechem anashim, "the bread of miserable men," i.e., mourners; probably, the funeral banquet.
entries.913b5c6cc1348d54e224b77abbd858a090bc7c11: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen31941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31942" type="x-p"/> At even my wife died - The prophet's wife was a type of the city, which was to him exceedingly dear. The death of his wife represented the destruction of the city by the Chaldeans; see <reference osisRef="Eze.24.21">Eze 24:21</reference>, where the temple is represented to be the desire of his eyes, as his wife was, <reference osisRef="Eze.24.16">Eze 24:16</reference>.
entries.deff756e399850143bb1a4c0772c222b43f2da76: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen31942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31943" type="x-p"/> Wilt thou not tell us - In the following verses he explains and applies the whole of what he had done and said.
entries.fb512819234a5ed35ea75ced04195739e8cb1c7c: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen31943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31944" type="x-p"/> In that day shall thy mouth be opened - What is, When some one who shall have escaped from Jerusalem, having arrived among the captives, shall inform them of the destruction of the city, the temple, the royal family, and the people at large; till then he might suppress his tears and lamentations. And we find from <reference osisRef="Eze.33.21">Eze 33:21</reference>, that one did actually escape from the city, and informed the prophet and his brethren in captivity that the city was smitten. <div eID="gen31944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31945" type="x-p"/> Thus he was not only a prophet to foretell such things, but he was also a sign or portent, shadowing them out by circumstances in his own person and family; and thus the prediction, agreeing so perfectly with the event, proved that the previous information was from the Lord.  <chapter eID="Ezek.24"/> <div eID="gen31945" type="x-p"/>

entries.d40d227bbef0cf2b9f2c9523e891c9769c0f9642: <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.1-Ezek.24.2">Eze 24:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen15008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15009" type="x-p"/> On the day on which the king of Babylon commenced the siege and blockade of Jerusalem, this event was revealed by God to Ezekiel on the Chaboras (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.1">Eze 24:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.2">Eze 24:2</reference>); and he was commanded to predict to the people through the medium of a parable the fate of the city and its inhabitants (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.3-Ezek.24.14">Eze 24:3-14</reference>). God then foretold to him the death of his own wife, and commanded him to show no sign of mourning on account of it. His wife died the following evening, and he did as he was commanded. When he was asked by the people the reason of this, he explained to them, that what he was doing was symbolical of the way in which they were to act when Jerusalem fell (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.15-Ezek.24.24">Eze 24:15-24</reference>). The fall would be announced to the prophet by a fugitive, and then he would no longer remain mute, but would speak to the people again (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.25-Ezek.24.27">Eze 24:25-27</reference>). - Apart, therefore, from the last three verses, this chapter contains two words of God, the first of which unfolds in a parable the approaching calamities, and the result of the siege of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.1-Ezek.24.14">Eze 24:1-14</reference>); whilst the second typifies by means of a sign the pain and mourning of Israel, namely, of the exiles at the destruction of the city with its sanctuary and its inhabitants. These two words of God, being connected together by their contents, were addressed to the prophet on the same day, and that, as the introduction (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.1">Eze 24:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.2">Eze 24:2</reference>) expressly observes, the day on which the siege of Jerusalem by the king of Babylon began.<hi type="italic">And the word of Jehovah came to me in the ninth year, in the tenth month, on the tenth of the month, saying,</hi> Eze 24:2. <hi type="italic">Son of man, write for thyself the name of the day, this same day! The king of Babylon has fallen upon Jerusalem this same day.</hi> - The date given, namely, the tenth day of the tenth month of the ninth year after the carrying away of Jehoiachin (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.2">Eze 1:2</reference>), or what is the same thing, of the reign of Zedekiah, who was appointed king in his stead, is mentioned in <reference osisRef="Jer.52.4">Jer 52:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.39.1">Jer 39:1</reference>, and 2Ki 25:1, as the day on which Nebuchadnezzar blockaded the city of Jerusalem by throwing up a rampart; and after the captivity this day was still kept as a fast-day in consequence (Zec 8:19). What was thus taking place at Jerusalem was revealed to Ezekiel on the Chaboras the very same day; and he was instructed to announce it to the exiles, “that they and the besieged might learn both from the time and the result, that the destruction of the city was not to be ascribed to chance or to the power of the Babylonians, but to the will of Him who had long ago foretold that, on account of the wickedness of the inhabitants, the city would be burned with fire; and that Ezekiel was a true prophet, because even when in Babylon, which was at so great a distance, he had known and had publicly announced the state of Jerusalem.” The definite character of this prediction cannot be changed into a <hi type="italic">vaticinium post eventum</hi>, either by arbitrary explanations of the words, or by the unfounded hypothesis proposed by Hitzig, that the day was not set down in this definite form till after the event. - Writing the name of the day is equivalent to making a note of the day. The reason for this is given in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.24.2">Eze 24:2</reference></hi>, namely, because Nebuchadnezzar had fallen upon Jerusalem on that very day. סמך signifies to support, hold up (his hand); and hence both here and in <reference osisRef="Ps.88.8">Psa 88:8</reference> the meaning to press violently upon anything. The rendering “to draw near,” which has been forced upon the word from the Syriac (Ges., Winer, and others), cannot be sustained.
entries.96863fa73d5b5ea35dd58c9e8c1765f95bd0a1f4: <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.3-Ezek.24.14">Eze 24:3-14</reference> <div eID="gen15009" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Parable of the Pot with the Boiling Pieces</title> <div sID="gen15010" type="x-p"/> Eze 24:3. <hi type="italic">And relate a parable to the rebellious house, and say to them, Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Set on the pot, set on and also pour water into it.</hi> Eze 24:4. <hi type="italic">Gather its pieces of flesh into it, all the good pieces, haunch and shoulder, fill it with choice bones.</hi> Eze 24:5. <hi type="italic">Take the choice of the flock, and also a pile of wood underneath for the bones; make it boil well, also cook its bones therein.</hi> Eze 24:6. <hi type="italic">Therefore, thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Woe! O city of murders! O pot in which is rust, and whose rust doth not depart from it; piece by piece fetch it out, the lot hath not fallen upon it.</hi> Eze 24:7. <hi type="italic">For her blood is in the midst of her; she hath placed it upon the naked rock; she hath not poured it upon the ground, that they might cover it with dust.</hi> Eze 24:8. <hi type="italic">To bring up fury, to take vengeance, I have made her blood come upon the naked rock, that it might not be covered.</hi> Eze 24:9. <hi type="italic">Therefore thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Woe to the city of murders! I also will make the pile of wood great.</hi> Eze 24:10. <hi type="italic">Heap up the wood, stir the fire, do the flesh thoroughly, make the broth boil, that the bones may also be cooked away.</hi> Eze 24:11. <hi type="italic">And set it empty upon the coals thereof, that its brass may become hot and glowing, that the uncleanness thereof may melt within it, its rust pass away.</hi> Eze 24:12. <hi type="italic">He hath exhausted the pains, and her great rust doth not go from her; into the fire with her rust!</hi> Eze 24:13. <hi type="italic">In thine uncleanness is abomination; because I have cleansed thee, and thou hast not become clean, thou wilt no more become clean from thy uncleanness, till I quiet my fury upon thee.</hi> Eze 24:14. <hi type="italic">I Jehovah have spoken it; it cometh, and I will do it; I will not cease, nor spare, nor let it repent me. According to thy ways, and according to thy deeds, shall they judge thee, is the saying of the Lord Jehovah.</hi> <div eID="gen15010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15011" type="x-p"/> The contents of these verses are called משׁל, a proverb or parable; and Ezekiel is to communicate them to the refractory generation. It follows from this that the ensuing act, which the prophet is commanded to perform, is not to be regarded as a symbolical act which he really carried out, but that the act forms the substance of the <hi type="italic">mâshâl</hi>, in other words, belongs to the parable itself. Consequently the interpretation of the parable in vv. 10ff. is clothed in the form of a thing actually done. The pot with the pieces of flesh and the bones, which are to be boiled in it and boiled away, represents Jerusalem with its inhabitants. The fire, with which they are boiled, is the fire of war, and the setting of the pot upon the fire is the commencement of the siege, by which the population of the city is to be boiled away like the flesh and bones in a pot. שׁפת is used, as in 2Ki 4:38, to signify the setting of a pot by or upon the fire. 'אסף וגו: put in its pieces all together. נתחיה, its pieces of flesh, i.e., the pieces belonging to the cooking-pot. These are defined still more minutely as the best of the pieces of flesh, and of these the thigh (haunch) and shoulder are mentioned as the most important pieces, to which the choicest of the bones are to be added. This is rendered still more emphatic by the further instruction to take the choice of the flock in addition to these.
